title: Verifier-Guided Prompting for Intent-to-Configuration Translation: A Preregistered NetOps Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory trial to test whether constrained prompting combined with a deterministic verifier-guided generate→verify→repair loop (one allowed repair) increases deterministic-verifier semantic-correctness when translating operator natural-language intents into low-level device configurations. Design: N=150 synthetic intents from a deterministic generator; execution-semantic: shared_initial_candidate (one initial sampled candidate reused across paired conditions); model = gpt-5-mini; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; guarded pipeline permitted ≤1 repair. Results (artifact-grounded): baseline = 149/150 (99.333%); guarded = 150/150 (100.0%); paired absolute difference = 0.006667 (≈0.67 percentage points); exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Provider accounting: completed episodes = 300; model_calls_used = 151; repair-stage invocations = 1. Interpretation: on this preregistered synthetic corpus and under shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded workflow produced a numerically negligible and statistically non-significant improvement over a near-ceiling baseline. We highlight the methodological lesson that preregistered NetOps trials need baseline-calibration pilots to avoid ceiling effects that invalidate preregistered power assumptions. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the supplied execution bundle referenced by the execution manifest.

sections.introduction:
Natural-language intent interfaces aim to reduce operator burden by letting humans express desired network changes as free text that is automatically translated into executable device configurations. Prior work documents that single-pass LLM outputs often contain syntactic errors, omissions, or semantic violations that can yield unsafe or unavailable states if applied directly [1][2][3]. A common mitigation is a generate→verify→repair architecture: an LLM produces a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks intent-level invariants or formalized constraints, and an automated repair (or human gate) corrects violations before execution [4][5]. Security analyses further motivate verifier-based gating because unguarded multi-tool agents can convert misleading textual claims into harmful actions [6].

Research question. After an autonomous literature review and preregistration we posed a confined confirmatory question: does constrained prompting (structured templates with explicit semantic slots) combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback materially increase verifier-level semantic correctness of NL→configuration translation versus an unconstrained baseline in a paired design? The trial (study_cand_2026_b2_v1) and its analysis plan were preregistered and frozen before any model outputs were observed.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifactized paired confirmatory trial on a deterministic synthetic corpus (N=150 paired intents) with explicit shared_initial_candidate execution semantics. (2) Artifact-backed outcomes reporting baseline = 149/150 and guarded = 150/150 (paired difference ≈0.67 pp; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02]). (3) A precise methodological recommendation: preregistered NetOps trials should include a short baseline-calibration pilot to avoid ceiling effects and must state generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate vs independent sampling) because semantics change the estimand and interpretation.
sections.related_work: Prior evaluations of NL→configuration and intent-to-configuration pipelines report that translating underspecified operator language into verifier-sound artifacts remains challenging; free-text prompts frequently produce omissions or incorrect sequencing that violate required invariants [1]. Systems that integrate deterministic verification into generation workflows (generate→verify→repair) report improved practical correctness for infrastructure-as-code and configuration-repair tasks, but effect sizes depend on baseline competence, verifier expressiveness, sampling semantics, and repair budget [2][3]. Formal network-verification tools (NetKAT/KATch family and related engines) provide deterministic oracles for reachability and policy checks and are commonly proposed as gating layers for LLM-generated configurations; their limited protocol coverage and scale constraints are known limitations [5]. Security analyses of agentic LLM pipelines demonstrate that unguarded multi-tool orchestration can be manipulated, motivating conservative, auditable verifier verdicts and gating [4]. Our experiment situates within this literature by preregistering a paired comparison with explicit sampling semantics and by executing a verifier-grounded binary endpoint.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The study was preregistered as study_cand_2026_b2_v1. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline evaluated with an exact two-sided McNemar test on deterministic-verifier pass/fail outcomes. The confirmatory sample specified N=150 distinct synthetic intents from a deterministic generator, deterministic prechecks (ambiguity detector, parser/unit-tests), and a power target of detecting an absolute +15 percentage-point improvement (~80% power) under conservative discordant-pair assumptions. The preregistration and analysis plan were frozen prior to any model-generated outputs.

Execution semantics and the critical mapping from preregistration to executed contrasts. The adapter enforced shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent exactly one initial model generation was produced and that identical sampled candidate was used in the paired evaluation of both conditions. The guarded pipeline was allowed at most one additional repair call only if the deterministic verifier failed that initial candidate. Mapping of preregistered labels to executed contrasts (explicit): the preregistration conceptually listed three conditions A (baseline free-text), B (constrained template), and C (constrained+verifier feedback) and two confirmatory hypotheses H1 (B vs A) and H2 (C vs B). Because the adapter enforced shared_initial_candidate sampling and the execution run recorded only one shared initial generation per task with at most one repair call, the only realized paired confirmatory contrast executed and analyzed as planned is guarded (C) versus baseline (A) on the identical initial candidate (the primary estimand). Constrained-only (B) was not executed as an independent first-pass condition in this run and therefore no independent B-vs-A or C-vs-B confirmatory contrasts appear in the archived analysis artifacts. This mapping is preregistered/adapter-enforced and is documented in the execution manifest (stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 150, repair: 1}) and provider accounting (model_calls_used = 151). No post-preregistration changes to the confirmatory analysis were made; the archived analysis follows the preregistered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor.

Model, sampling, validator, and scoring. Declared model: gpt-5-mini (provider record: openai_responses); model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and temperature = null (unset). Because no numeric temperature or fixed random seed was imposed, independent-session nondeterminism is possible; sampling semantics were handled explicitly by the shared_initial_candidate enforcement. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0) applied a full_intent_constraint_validation rule returning a boolean pass/fail, normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, and violation codes. The binary pass/fail was the primary endpoint. The adapter performed mapping unit-tests and verifier-coverage checks before batch execution; tasks failing prechecks would have been excluded per the preregistered exclusion rules (none were excluded in the archived run).

Execution accounting, inclusion/exclusion, and analysis procedures. Planned episodes: 300 (150 intents × 2 conditions); completed_episode_count = 300; complete_pair_count = 150. Provider-call budget: maximum_model_calls = 300; model_calls_used = 151. Repair budget: at most one repair invocation per intent; observed repair-stage invocations = 1. Primary analysis: exact McNemar two-sided test on paired contingency counts (n_11, n_10, n_01, n_00) plus a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Missingness: preregistered policy excluded incomplete pairs from the primary test (complete_pair_primary); sensitivity analyses treating missing guarded outputs as failures were preregistered but not invoked because no model-call failures occurred. All analysis code and artifacts are archived.
sections.results:
Execution audit and provider accounting. The run completed as planned: completed_episode_count = 300 and complete_pair_count = 150. Provider-call accounting: model_calls_used = 151; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 151; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0; cache_miss_count = 151. Stage-level counts: shared_initial_generation = 150 and repair = 1. Contamination checks and mapping unit-tests passed; contamination_summary.csv records zero flags.

Primary numerical outcomes (artifact-grounded). Paired contingency counts (guarded × baseline): n_11 = 149 (both-pass), n_10 = 1 (guarded-only-pass), n_01 = 0 (baseline-only-pass), n_00 = 0 (both-fail). Per-condition success rates: baseline_success_rate = 149/150 = 0.9933333333333333; guarded_success_rate = 150/150 = 1.0. Estimated paired absolute difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00666666666666671 (≈0.67 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729). These values are reported verbatim from analysis/results.json and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv archived in the execution bundle.

Repair diagnostics and revision iterations. Only a single guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150). That single repair converted one initially failing candidate into a passing configuration under the deterministic verifier. Median revision iterations for guarded episodes = 0 (IQR = 0). Representative validator traces (e.g., tasks 000001–000006) are archived and include parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes, normalized_configuration, and valid flags.

Representative example. Task-000001 (generator_seed = 1) intent: "Migrate edge1 to VLAN 30 and MTU 1600. For safety, shut edge1 down before changing either VLAN or MTU, then restore it to admin up. Do not modify any other interface." Shared-initial and both condition responses returned the expected four-command sequence. Validator diagnostics for task-000001: parsed_command_count = 4; required_command_count = 4; observed_touched_field_count = 3; valid = true. Shared-initial candidate and normalized_configuration strings are archived in provider and scorer traces.

Sensitivity and missingness. No model-call failures or parse failures occurred; the preregistered sensitivity analysis treating missing guarded outputs as failures was therefore not invoked. No confirmatory exclusions were applied.
sections.discussion:
Ceiling effect and inferential consequence. The preregistered power calculation assumed a substantially lower baseline; the observed baseline_success_rate = 0.9933 left essentially no headroom for the guarded repair to produce a large absolute improvement. This ceiling effect undermined the preregistered detectable-effect assumptions (target = +15 percentage points) and left minimal discordant-pair information (only one discordant pair), so the confirmatory McNemar test provides no evidence of a meaningful guarded benefit under this estimand. We therefore recommend that preregistered NetOps trials include a short baseline-calibration pilot (20–40 tasks sampled from the planned generator and prompt style) to estimate baseline competence and adjust final N or task difficulty accordingly.

Sampling semantics, estimand interpretation, and design trade-offs. The shared_initial_candidate enforcement makes the guarded−baseline contrast a pure marginal-repair estimand: it measures the benefit of applying at most one repair to a fixed first-pass candidate. Alternative semantics (independent per-condition sampling or multi-draw ensembles) address different operational questions (expected pass rates when each pipeline draws independently or when re-sampling is permitted) and typically increase observable discordance at the cost of additional model calls and latency. Practitioners must align sampling semantics and repair budgets with deployment constraints and incorporate these choices into power planning.

Repair budgets, operational cost, and diminishing returns. Provider accounting quantifies the guarded design cost under a one-repair budget: model_calls_used = 151 and repair-stage invocations = 1. With a near-ceiling baseline, repairs are rarely invoked and marginal cost per success-conversion is high. In lower-baseline regimes repairs convert more failures but yield diminishing returns as repair count increases; estimating per-repair marginal gains requires multi-arm experiments that vary allowed repair counts.

Operational affordances beyond binary pass/fail. Deterministic validators return normalized configurations, violation codes, and fine-grained diagnostics that aid triage, auditing, and human-in-the-loop repair even when verifier-pass differences are small. Guarded pipelines can therefore improve operational observability and reduce human triage effort independent of marginal verifier-pass improvements on tightly specified corpora.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: adapter-enforced budgets and provider audits mitigated cross-condition leakage and mapping unit-tests reduced parser failures. Construct validity: the deterministic verifier is a proxy for semantic correctness and depends on mapping code and verifier coverage; uncovered coverage gaps remain a potential bias. External validity: experiments used a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic small topologies (4–32 nodes); results do not generalize to other models or production-scale heterogeneous networks. Security: adversarial prompt-injection and adversary-driven intents were not evaluated in this confirmatory trial and remain separate research directions.

Practical prescriptions. Based on artifact-grounded outcomes we recommend: (1) baseline-calibration pilots before committing to confirmatory N; (2) explicit preregistration of generation semantics and repair budgets; (3) multi-arm designs that vary repair budgets and sampling semantics to estimate cost–benefit frontiers; (4) inclusion of provider-call accounting in power and cost planning; and (5) staged scaling with deterministic mapping unit-tests and verifier-coverage checks. The archived execution manifest and representative task seeds provide concrete material to run such follow-up arms reproducibly.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired confirmatory trial comparing baseline free-text prompting with constrained-template prompting plus a single verifier-guided repair under shared_initial_candidate semantics. On a deterministic synthetic corpus with gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 the guarded pipeline increased verifier pass rate from 149/150 to 150/150 (≈0.67 pp), a numerically tiny and statistically non-significant difference (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02]). The principal scientific lesson is methodological: preregistered NetOps trials should include brief baseline-calibration pilots to avoid ceiling effects and preserve inferential validity. Technically, our artifacts bound the marginal benefit of a one-repair guarded pipeline under shared_initial_candidate semantics; evaluating independent-sampling semantics, larger repair budgets, model diversity, and production-scale topologies remains important future work.

limitations: Single-model constraint: experiments used only gpt-5-mini; results do not generalize across models or sizes.

Synthetic corpus and scale: tasks were programmatically generated and limited to verifier-capable toy-to-small topologies (4–32 nodes); external validity to production WANs and heterogeneous vendor CLIs is untested.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract limited repair budget to at most one guarded repair call per intent; different generation semantics or multiple-repair budgets may yield different outcomes.

Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch: baseline correctness was far higher than the pilot assumptions used for power calculations (planned detectable effect = 15 percentage points), reducing the trial's ability to demonstrate benefit and illustrating sensitivity to baseline calibration.

Verifier coverage and specification translation: the study measures deterministic validator pass/fail on the preregistered invariants but does not claim safety guarantees beyond the deterministic validator's modeled properties.

Security and adversarial robustness: the experiment did not evaluate adversarial prompt-injection or adversary-driven intents; separate targeted studies are required to assess claim-to-action vulnerabilities in agentic NetOps workflows.
